♻ ☆ Attention over noisy examples: generalization and memorization in the exponential Hopfield network
Francesco Alemanno
In Hebbian learning from examples, a Hopfield network retrieves archetypes seen only through noisy examples. We study it in the exponential Hopfield model: one softmax attention step with the unlabelled examples as keys. A signal-to-noise analysis gives the overlap with an unseen archetype in closed form: a majority-rule law in which an attention entropy replaces the dataset entropy. At high temperature the archetype is lost in the crosstalk; at low temperature the softmax freezes on the closest training example, as in a random energy model, and the layer memorizes. In between, in a window widening with the square root of the network size, the layer pools the examples of the correct class and retrieves the unseen archetype as well as their majority vote allows, at any fixed load. On structured datasets, such as MNIST and fashion-MNIST, the best accuracy lies beyond the freezing.

[1]. We empirically evaluate seven merging methods on Mistral-7B models across official GSM8K (1,319 questions) and MMLU (14,042 questions, 57 subjects) benchmarks. Our structured approach achieves a 49.5% reduction in effective search space. Results reveal that all tested merging methods fail to surpass the stronger source model on official benchmarks, with TIES (13.72%) and DELLA (4.12%) performing catastrophically on GSM8K. Notably, DELLA scores below even the base model (6.67%), demonstrating that standard parameter space methods fail when merging base and instruction-tuned models. We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable. We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure. Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
☆ Envy-Free Randomized Apportionment
Francesco La Commare, Jamie Tucker-Foltz, Victor Verdugo
The United States allocates representatives to each state in proportion to its population, while many parliamentary democracies select representatives from party lists in proportion to the number of votes each party receives. In both settings, the legislature's small size necessitates rounding to the nearest whole number of seats. Recent work has shown a plethora of ways to randomly round seat shares to achieve perfect ex ante fairness. As a result, party (state) $i$ may have a larger number of votes (population) than party $j$ but receive fewer seats. In this case, we say that party $i$ envies party $j$. We investigate the extent to which such envy is avoidable. Specifically, we seek to design apportionment rules that minimize the expected number of envious pairs $(i, j)$. If the expectation is zero, we say that the seat allocation is envy-free. On the negative side, we show that any $n$-party apportionment rule that ignores lower quotas (the floors of the deserved number of seats for each party) suffers from a worst-case envy of $Θ(n^2)$, even on instances where an envy-free allocation exists. All previously studied apportionment rules fall into this class and thus do a poor job of minimizing envy. In the case where all lower quotas are equal, we prove that all allocations have the same expected envy. In the general case, we we introduce a general polynomial-time LP framework for a large class of apportionment objectives, including minimizing the expectation and variance of envy, by efficiently solving the separation problem on the dual. Finally, we empirically demonstrate that envy-free allocations exist very frequently, including in every historical instance from the US decennial census. Taken together, these results provide a clear recipe for implementing randomized apportionment in a less objectionable way in practice.
☆ Coopshift: Post-Training Amplifies The Memory Curse In LLM Cooperation
Jiayuan Liu, Shiyi Du, Tianqin Li, Emanuel Tewolde, Keyang Xuan, Vincent Conitzer
How does post-training change cooperation during repeated interaction? Within each of seven released model lineages, we compare pretrained (Base), supervised fine-tuned (SFT), and subsequent preference- or reward-optimized (Aligned) checkpoints across seven social dilemmas. Copies of each checkpoint play one another for 200 rounds, with visible history limited to the last two or forty rounds. The memory curse refers to lower cooperation when agents can see more past rounds. Our central finding is that post-training amplifies this decline. Averaged across the six binary-action games, expanding visible history reduces cooperation at every SFT and Aligned checkpoint. At each post-trained stage, these declines exceed Base's in six of seven lineages. Most of this average amplification is already present at SFT. With long history, both post-trained stages also cooperate less than Base on average in each binary-action game. In the symmetric binary games, their fitted cooperation rates fall more steeply on average than Base's as per-round cooperation costs rise, benefits fall, or noncooperation becomes more rewarding. The difference in cooperation rates between Aligned and SFT also changes from one-shot decisions to repeated play. When given the same past records, their choices depend on whether the instructions describe a final round or possible future interaction. Post-training evaluation should therefore go beyond isolated choices to assess whether cooperation is sustained in repeated interaction and how it depends on payoffs and visible history.
☆ Revisiting the Fairness of Pure Nash Equilibria of Round-Robin
Georgios Amanatidis, Haris Aziz, Georgios Birmpas, Federico Fusco, Stefano Leonardi, Rebecca Reiffenhäuser
We prove that for additive valuations, not every pure Nash equilibrium of the Round-Robin mechanism induces an allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1) with respect to the agents' true valuations. This corrects an earlier claim of Amanatidis et al. (WINE 2021; Math. Oper. Res. 2024). On the positive side, every pure Nash equilibrium of every fixed recursively balanced picking sequence mechanism induces an allocation that is $1/2$-EF1 and proportional up to one good (PROP1). We prove the approximate EF1 guarantee through a potential function comparing two executions, and the proportionality guarantee via a deviation that preserves the agent's most valuable goods. We also give a family of Round Robin equilibria showing that it is not possible to have a strictly better guarantee than $2/3$-EF1 for all equilibria.
comment: Corrects the claim in arXiv:2109.08644 (WINE 2021; Math. Oper. Res. 49(4), 2024) that every pure Nash equilibrium of Round-Robin is EF1. We give a counterexample, identify the step of the original proof that fails, and show that every pure Nash equilibrium is 1/2-EF1 and PROP1, also for recursively balanced picking sequences
☆ Uniform-Price Mechanism Design for Automated Market Makers
Zhike Peng
Automated market makers (AMMs) are central to decentralized exchanges, but their reserve curves make mechanism design different from classical double auctions. We study a batch double auction with buyers, sellers, and a liquidity-nondecreasing AMM: post-trade reserves must have weakly larger product than the initial reserves. Each user has two-dimensional private information: a unit value and a demand or supply quantity. User trades clear at one uniform price subject to AMM feasibility. The objective is user-side trading volume, benchmarked against the optimal feasible individually rational (IR) uniform-price allocation. We give a randomized uniform-price mechanism based on binary quantity buckets. It randomly chooses one of three clearing modes: peer-to-peer matching, AMM sales to buyers, and seller sales to the AMM. Every deterministic realization of the mechanism is ex-post feasible and satisfies IR and weak quantity incentive compatibility: conditional on any quantity report, truthful unit-value reporting is dominant whenever it gives a non-negative utility, no unit-value deviation gives a positive utility if the truthful one doesn't, and users cannot benefit by under-reporting the quantity together with their truthful unit value. Let $V^\ast$ be the optimal feasible IR uniform-price volume without incentive constraints, and let $γ=\bar q/\underline q$, where $\bar q$ and $\underline q$ are the quantity-domain bounds. For $γ\ge1$, the mechanism achieves an expected trading volume of $ Ω(1/(1+\logγ)^2)V^\ast - O(\bar q). $ We also show that full incentive compatibility over the two-dimensional type space forces a worst-case approximation ratio of $O(1/γ)$ at every prescribed initial reserve ratio, even when both AMM reserves are scaled by an arbitrarily large common factor and the optimal volume $V^\ast$ is arbitrarily large relative to $\bar q$.
comment: 22 pages. Full version of a paper accepted at IJTCS-FAW 2026
☆ Contracting with an Agent under Model Mismatch
Elif Yılmaz, Jakub Tłuczek, Victor Villin, Christos Dimitrakakis
In the classical principal-agent setting, the principal delegates some task to the agent, who receives a payment conditioned on the outcome of the task, which in turn benefits the principal. To align their objectives, the principal designs a contract that incentivizes the agent to take actions beneficial to the principal. In practice, however, the agent may act under misspecified beliefs about the underlying environment, leading to systematically suboptimal decisions. In this work, we study this problem through a principal-agent Markov Decision Process (PAMDP), in which the principal repeatedly interacts with an agent whose transition model may differ from the true environment dynamics. The principal has access to the true transition model and designs contracts that account for the agent's belief and incentives. We characterize contract design under model mismatch and develop a framework that enables the principal to induce desirable long-term benefits even though the agent has a potentially inaccurate understanding of the environment.
☆ Bayesian Learning of Parametric Mean Field Games with Common Noise
Grégoire Lambrecht, Mathieu Laurière
We study the inverse problem of recovering unknown parameters governing the dynamics and rewards of Mean Field Games (MFGs) from partial observations of population trajectories, made stochastic by common noise. The observer seeks to recover a consistent parameter $θ$ via Bayesian inference, facing the challenge that evaluating the likelihood requires solving a new Nash equilibrium (NE) for each candidate $θ$. Due to common noise, the mean-field evolution is stochastic and equilibrium policies are population dependent, which makes solving for each parameter computationally expensive. To overcome this, we introduce the Bayesian-Extended Mean Field Game (BE-MFG), whose single NE simultaneously encodes equilibrium policies for all parameters, enabling efficient learning of the conditional density of mean-field trajectories. We formalize parameter consistency and identifiability in MFGs with common noise and investigate conditions under which consistent parameter recovery is guaranteed. On three synthetic environments of various complexity, we recover the ground-truth parameter accurately from a small number of partial, stochastic observations, outperforming an adaptation of inverse reinforcement learning for MFGs. A fourth experiment, on public electricity market data, suggests that the approach can also be applied to real-world data.
☆ Trembling toward Duverger: Convergence and Cycles in Synchronous Plurality Dynamics
Maximilian Weigel, Damien Berriaud, Roger Wattenhofer
Duverger's law states that plurality elections tend to concentrate support on two candidates. Pivotal-voter models typically derive this from aggregate uncertainty about votes, so that two-candidate competition emerges in the limit of large electorates. We instead propose a model for a fixed, finite population. A poll reveals the current support counts, and each voter best responds under trembling-hand beliefs, assuming that every other voter may deviate with a small probability. Starting from truthful votes, we show that a single update typically suffices for the dynamics to converge to a stable profile in which every voter supports her preferred candidate among the two poll leaders. For any number of candidates and any full-support tremble belief, a four-vote lead of the runner-up over all lower candidates suffices; for three candidates, a lead of two suffices. As a consequence, under random preferences, Duverger's law emerges after one update with probability $1-\mathcal O(N^{-1/2})$. While these results may suggest that the dynamics always settle, convergence can fail. Mild period-two cycles already arise, with a few voters swapping ballots around an otherwise stable profile. We show that substantially richer behavior is possible, even with three candidates. Period-three cycles arise with six voters changing their ballots, and no such cycle can involve fewer than four. Cycles can also alternate the plurality winner. Moreover, larger electorates support ever longer cycles: for every odd $\ell\geq3$, truthful voting can lead to a cycle whose vote counts repeat every $\ell$ rounds and whose full ballot profile repeats every $2\ell$ rounds.
comment: 19 pages, 2 figures
☆ Proportionality in Ranking Compression NeurIPS
Daniel Halpern, Xinyu Liu, Evi Micha, Yu Peng Ng, Warut Suksompong
Motivated by applications in reinforcement learning from human feedback, we consider a setting where a given collection of rankings needs to be compressed into a smaller collection of rankings. This can also be seen as a combination of two fundamental social choice frameworks: ranking aggregation and multiwinner voting. We propose three proportionality notions that capture different types of representation in this setting: positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC). On the one hand, we show that positional proportionality and PSC are always satisfiable for any input rankings and target compression size, and a desired output can be found in polynomial time. On the other hand, we prove that pairwise proportionality cannot be satisfied in general, but can nevertheless be attained when the input rankings are single-peaked or single-crossing.
comment: Appears in the 40th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2026
☆ On the Convergence of Iterated Round Robin
Maxime Lucet, Henri Surugue, Nawal Benabbou, Aurélie Beynier, Nicolas Maudet, Arianna Novaro
Round Robin (RR) is a simple and widely used picking sequence mechanism for allocating indivisible goods, known to guarantee envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) when preferences are additive. Despite being manipulable (meaning that agents may have an incentive to strategically misreport their preferences), it is known to always admit at least one pure Nash equilibrium. In this paper, we study an iterated variant of RR, in which agents observe the outcome of the mechanism at each iteration and may revise their reported preferences through a best-response dynamics. We first consider a full-information setting, where agents observe both the outcome and the reported preferences of all the agents. In this setting, we show that cycles can occur even under strong restrictions on the manipulations carried out by the agents. We nonetheless identify a natural restriction (item-preserving swaps), under which convergence to a pure Nash equilibrium is guaranteed to exist for any number of agents and items. We also show that restricting to adjacent swaps guarantees convergence for two agents and a limited number of items, leaving the question open for unbounded number of items. We then turn to a partial-information setting, in which agents only observe the resulting allocation and must then infer the preference profiles of the others assuming consistency with the RR sequence. We study three behaviours guiding the agents when deciding how to manipulate under uncertainty on the other agents' preferences. We show that two of the studied behaviours, despite being quite natural, may cycle while a more cautious rule guarantees iterated RR to be strategyproof.
☆ Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma
Trung-Kiet Huynh, Dao-Sy Duy-Minh, Chi-Nguyen Tran, Phu-Hoa Pham, Phu-Quy Nguyen-Lam, Le Hong Trang, The Anh Han
Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. In a collective-risk dilemma game (CRG), six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds; if the pool falls short of its target, a catastrophe may destroy their remaining resources. Four models contributed approximately an equal share at every positive risk level, and four of the five also contributed when risk was zero, even though contributing could not improve their payoff. Explicitly stating that only the agent's own payoff mattered reduced zero-risk contributions for most models, while a more neutral prompt did not. Several models correctly identified which action offered the higher expected payoff at different risk levels, yet their contributions changed little. Against fixed partners, no model consistently chose the payoff-maximising response, and in mixed-model groups, a single agent's shortfall in the final round could cause an otherwise successful group to fail. Payoff-based selection also depended on population composition: in a single six-agent group, it favoured the model that contributed least and reduced group success, whereas in larger, randomly mixed populations, it favoured an exact fair-share model at moderate and high risk. These findings show that cooperative self-play alone is not evidence of strategic adaptability. Consistent with a machine-behaviour approach, evaluations of agents in multi-agent systems should test how they respond to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 50-page supplementary material appended
☆ The Source of Data Value: Consumer Disclosure, Access Design, and Platform Monetization
Hexiao Liu, Lijian Lu, Mingzheng Wang
Digital marketplaces increasingly earn revenue from transaction commissions and seller-facing data services. Sellers may purchase data to increase revenue or avoid competing with an informed rival. We examine how consumer disclosure rights shape these motives and the platform's incentive to provide data. We develop a game-theoretic model of a commissioned platform, two differentiated sellers, and privacy-sensitive consumers. Data generates value through bilateral sales-revenue gains and competition threats arising from asymmetric access. Under mandatory collection, the platform can monetize defensive adoption, even when bilateral personalization reduces seller revenue. Under voluntary disclosure, anonymous purchasing and strictly positive privacy costs make unilateral disclosure unattractive in the baseline. Exclusive access thus yields no usable information, restores sellers' no-data rejection payoffs, and eliminates defensive fees. Profitable provision therefore requires nonnegative bilateral revenue gains. Under full fee extraction, sellers retain their no-data net profits. This revenue alignment does not guarantee welfare gains: additional transactions may benefit consumers, whereas segmentation in an already covered market can raise anonymous prices and reduce welfare. Capping anonymous offers at their no-data benchmark protects individual consumers and limits positive-mass provision to the transaction-creation region. Extensions consider access choice, heterogeneous privacy costs, imperfect identification, and limited contractual credibility. Platforms should evaluate data services based on both bilateral-use and seller-rejection outcomes, and sellers should distinguish revenue-enhancing from defensive investments. Regulators should distinguish equal-access rules from effective consumer control and monitor pricing in anonymous channels.
☆ Optimally Curating an Event IJCAI 2026
MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Sebastien Lahaie, Mohammad Mahdavi, Suho Shin
We study the optimal design of a self-financing event, a problem that requires balancing the recruitment of costly, positive-value participants with revenue-generating agents who may impose negative values on the event. We introduce a novel two-sided mechanism design framework with plus agents equipped with private costs and positive impact, and minus agents with private values and negative impact upon inclusion in the event, to maximize the overall quality of the event under a budget-balanced (BB) constraint so that the designer does not run a deficit. We conduct a comprehensive study on the theory of optimal event curation on various utility functions. For additive utility, we fully characterize the optimal incentive-compatible Bayesian mechanism under both the ex-ante and ex-post BB constraints. For submodular utility, we propose an ex-ante BB mechanism that achieves a constant-factor approximation to the optimal Bayesian mechanism.
comment: Appeared at IJCAI 2026
☆ Anytime Contracts for AI Services
Boris Velasevic, Eden Saig, Eric Mazumdar
AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

♻ ☆ Partition function form games with probabilistic beliefs
Paraskevas V. Lekeas, Giorgos Stamatopoulos
We revisit games in partition function form, i.e. cooperative games where the payoff of a coalition depends on the partition of the entire set of players. We assume that each coalition computes its worth having probabilistic beliefs over the coalitional behavior of the outsiders, i.e., it assigns various probability distributions over the set of partitions that the outsiders can form. These beliefs are not necessarily consistent with respect to the actual choices of the outsiders. We apply this framework to symmetric partition function form games characterized by either positive or negative externalities and we derive conditions on coalitional beliefs that guarantee the non-emptiness of the core of the induced games.
♻ ☆ Should the Timing of Inspections be Predictable?
Ian Ball, Jan Knoepfle
A principal hires an agent to work on a long-term project that culminates in a breakthrough or a breakdown. At each time, the agent privately chooses to work or shirk. Working increases the arrival rate of breakthroughs and decreases the arrival rate of breakdowns. To motivate the agent to work, the principal conducts costly inspections. She fires the agent if shirking is detected. We characterize the principal's optimal inspection policy. Predictable inspections are optimal if work primarily generates breakthroughs. Random inspections are typically optimal if work primarily prevents breakdowns. Crucially, the agent's actions affect the curvature of the project's survival probability, which determines his induced risk attitude over the timing of planned inspections.
♻ ☆ Delegate Pricing to Algorithms: When Slow and Steady Wins the Race
Galit Ashkenazi-Golan, Edward Plumb, Clemens Possnig, Yufei Zhang
We study the strategic design of learning algorithms in a canonical continuous-time pricing game. We introduce a meta-game in which firms select learning rates for a gradient dynamic, evaluating payoffs as the discounted sum of profits accrued along the entire learning path. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy driven by stage-game incentives: if the stage game exhibits strategic substitutability, each firm strictly prefers faster learning. Under strategic complementarity, however, an excessively fast algorithm accelerates the rival's competitive response, destroying transitional profit margins. Even though the competitive price is a dominant action in the stage game and convergence to this price is guaranteed, we prove that firms design sluggish algorithms in equilibrium.
♻ ☆ Robustness in Mechanism Design
Jason Hartline
The article reviews the robust design and analysis of auctions, focusing on the predominant paradigm in the computer science literature, which quantifies robustness by the worst-case, over environments, ratio between the robust auction's performance and that of an optimal auction for the environment. Applications include robust analysis of canonical auctions such as the first-price auction for the welfare objective, prior-robust auction design for the revenue objective, and prior-robust design of exchange mechanisms for the gains-from-trade objective. Finally, the revelation principle is not without loss in robust mechanism design. The potential loss can be quantified by the revelation gap, the fraction of the optimal robust guarantee that is lost when restricting from all mechanisms to revelation mechanisms.
comment: This is a preprint of a review article that is accepted to appear in the Annual Review of Economics in August of 2027. It contains an additional section on the revelation gap that, for space reasons, was mostly removed from the published version
♻ ☆ Best-of-Both-Worlds Guarantees with Fairer Endings
Telikepalli Kavitha, Surya Panchapakesan, Rohit Vaish, Vignesh Viswanathan, Jatin Yadav
We study best-of-both-worlds guarantees for the fair division of indivisible goods. Prior work has shown that under additive valuations, there always exists a randomized allocation that is ex-ante stochastic-dominance envy-free (sd-EF) and ex-post envy-free up to one good (EF1). Our work is motivated by the goal of achieving stronger ex-post fairness guarantees such as envy-freeness up to any good (EFX). Towards this goal, we make the following contributions: (i) Our first set of results considers a subdomain of additive valuations called \textit{lexicographic} preferences. On the negative side, we show that ex-ante sd-EF is fundamentally in conflict with ex-post EFX, prompting a relaxation in the ex-ante benchmark. On the positive side, we present a polynomial time algorithm that achieves ex-ante $\max\{1-\frac{2}{n+1},\,\frac{9}{10}\}$-EF and ex-post EFX and Pareto optimality, where $n$ is the number of agents. Our algorithm uses a novel dependent rounding technique that, to the best of our knowledge, is its first application in fair division. (ii) Our second set of results concerns beyond-additive valuations. We present a pseudopolynomial time algorithm for \textit{monotone} valuations that achieves $\frac{1}{2}$-EF and ex-post EFX-with-charity. For \textit{subadditive} valuations, we achieve ex-ante $\frac{1}{3}$-EF and ex-post $\frac{1}{2}$-EFX.

♻ ☆ RSD-Poker: Structure-Adaptive and Shift-Robust Risk-Utility Certification for Residual Policies in Imperfect-Information Games

Each candidate-group pair receives a weighted simultaneous upper certificate for anchor-relative risk and a lower certificate for weak-response utility. A robust group-to-candidate map is then selected over a predeclared uncertainty set of deployment group proportions. Under independent calibration units drawn from each frozen group's law, a candidate bank and partition fixed before calibration, and invariant within-group conditionals, the selected map satisfies its declared mixture-robust risk budget and utility certificate with probability at least $1-ζ_{risk}-ζ_{util}$. The information contract supports both a teacher-backed transform and a teacher-free observation-only student. The retained deterministic 24-state audit remains an exact replay diagnostic: empirical-zero selects $α=0.08$, raising the weak-response proxy from 4.2082 to 4.2889 with $0/12$ held-out threshold crossings. On stratified held-out states, the learned-partition dual selector raises weak utility from 4.4074 under global dual certification to 4.4936 and lowers held-out violation from 0.0215 to 0.0078; its mixture-robust variant reaches violation 0.0059. Across five observation-only checkpoints, risk-calibrated residuals attain weak utility $4.3659\pm0.0177$ and violation rate $0.0178\pm0.0057$.

♻ ☆ OSCC: Certified Observation-Safe Coupling Optimization for Gradient-Noise Control in Imperfect-Information Learning

Coupled rollouts can reduce the noise of counterfactual action comparisons, but two issues prevent standard common-random-number constructions from serving as a general learning primitive in imperfect-information environments. First, an invalid coupling may expose hidden state, synchronize endogenous policy randomness, or misalign chance events after counterfactual histories diverge. Second, in multi-action policy optimization, lower return-contrast variance is not by itself the relevant objective: the optimizer depends on the return covariance matrix after projection through the local policy-gradient geometry. We derive a gradient-aware coupling criterion showing that, for marginal-preserving couplings, policy-gradient noise changes are determined by policy-Jacobian-weighted off-diagonal return covariance. This motivates OSCC-Select, a calibration-only selector that chooses among independent, root-only, continuation-only, and fully coupled rollouts using separate safety and gain certificates. Its gain target combines projected gradient noise with measured physical sampling cost and falls back to independent sampling whenever a simultaneous lower confidence bound does not certify improvement. On 100,000 fixed-root Leduc comparisons, the fully coupled CP-GRPO instantiation reduces return-contrast variance from 41.1158 to 18.1441, a 55.87% reduction, while preserving the declared branch marginals. With three actions, OSCC-Select chooses continuation coupling and attains gradient-noise trace 0.0783 versus 0.0917 for return-variance selection. Increasing calibration from 64 to 2,048 groups raises certification from 0.327 to 0.995.

Opponent histories can mislead after behavioral shifts. SafeAdapt-Poker formulates budgeted adaptation under opponent shift as a dual-counterfactual sequential-control problem using only information available before each decision. At each decision the controller asks two distinct questions: what local downside a deviation from the frozen anchor would induce under matched legal continuations, and what future adaptation value would be lost by consuming part of the remaining deviation budget now. The first question is answered by a monotone strategic-risk model over deviation intensity; the second by a paired budget-state continuation model that prices current budget consumption. The controller selects among support-preserving candidate deviations by trading immediate adaptation value against these two quantities, a pathwise cumulative-KL ledger bounds total anchor-relative deviation, and a finite family of frozen controllers is screened on complete paired calibration sessions before held-out interaction. A finite-candidate perturbation bound shows that the allocation objective degrades continuously with continuation-value estimation error. Evaluation covers exact-game exploitation and safety, four opponent shifts, local-risk calibration, delayed-opportunity allocation, direct opportunity-value estimation, value-error robustness, factorial mechanism attribution, budget sensitivity, abstract-HUNL cross-play, and player/time-held-out public-history behavior. On exact Leduc the full controller attains a matched weak-pool gain of +0.0718 with a worst-opponent delta of -0.0126, raises delayed-opportunity capture from 0.6318 under myopic allocation to 0.7841 under the same session budget, and reaches +42.7 mbb/hand in abstract-HUNL cross-play; the retained public-history screen reports 0.5820 action accuracy and 0.9277 log loss versus 0.5039 and 0.9778 for a public prior.

♻ ☆ Adverse Effects of V2V Adoption on Road Safety
Zhenqi Liu, Philip N. Brown, Keith Paarporn
Vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication is expected to improve road safety and reduce congestion. However, prior work shows that V2V information sharing under partial adoption may increase congestion and decrease safety. We study whether increasing V2V adoption itself affects road safety. We propose a corrected version of an existing model and analyze its behavior under varying adoption levels. We show that, in some cases, increased V2V adoption can increase accident probability. However, under an optimal signaling policy, the system can ensure that accident probability is non-increasing in the adoption level.

☆ Algorithm Modelization: Transforming Optimization Algorithms into Evolvable Intelligence
Jian Yao, Zhiyao Zhang, Yichen Li, Xingyu Wu, Kay Chen Tan
Can algorithms be learned and evolved as models, rather than repeatedly redesigned as programs? We explore this question by introducing Algorithm Modelization, a new paradigm that turns iterative algorithms into trainable models. Its central idea is to regard algorithm execution trajectories as computational experience: by learning how algorithmic states evolve over iterations, a model can internalize the knowledge embodied in existing algorithms, reproduce their computational behaviors, and further evolve beyond them through training. As a first realization of this paradigm, we modelize iterative optimization as an autoregressive process, where preceding generations constitute the computational context for generating the next population. We develop a dimension-independent population-temporal architecture to capture both population interactions and iterative dynamics, together with an imitation-to-surpassing learning framework that first acquires algorithmic knowledge from heterogeneous teachers and then improves the resulting optimizer directly through optimization feedback. The modelized optimizer consequently goes beyond reproducing individual algorithms: it consolidates heterogeneous search knowledge into a single trainable model, achieves stronger optimization capability through subsequent improvement, and generalizes its acquired knowledge across problems and substantially larger unseen dimensions. More fundamentally, Algorithm Modelization makes algorithmic capability accumulable through learning, where new algorithms and problem-solving experience can become training resources for progressively improving the model. Our results establish a promising path from manually designed algorithms toward general algorithm models that learn, generalize, and evolve from computational experience.
☆ Wavelength Diversity Expands the Expressive Power of Optical Computing
Shiqi Chen, Che-Yung Shen, Parnian Ghapandar Kashani, Yongkang Cheng, Aydogan Ozcan
Universal function approximation underpins neural networks' capacity to represent nonlinear relationships, but realizing this capability in optical hardware requires engineering the computational features encoded in light. Here, we show that wavelength diversity enhances optical function-approximation expressivity through wavelength-scaled Fourier features generated by a shared phase encoder, without increasing the number of input-encoded harmonics. Multiple wavelengths contribute to the representation of each output function rather than merely serving as independent computational channels. We establish theoretical scaling laws and approximation-error bounds, revealing that, for nondispersive encoders, the spectral endpoints determine the accessible computational bandwidth, while intermediate illumination wavelengths enrich the available harmonics within that bandwidth. On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs) consume far less energy than artificial neural networks (ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them without retraining and, like those for ANNs, minimize numerical errors such as the mean squared error (MSE). In an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas errors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss. We therefore propose SpikeQ, a spike-guided PTQ framework. For weights, we select the level of each weight by simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their spike errors. For membrane potentials, most existing methods quantize the state after the reset, whereas neuromorphic chips compare the threshold with the membrane potential stored at a fixed bit width. We target this pre-fire quantization and build a reset-aware grid that places the threshold on a rounding boundary, so rounding never flips the spike at the current time step. We evaluate SpikeQ on seven benchmarks of image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. With 2-bit pre-fire membrane potentials, every existing grid collapses, whereas SpikeQ retains most of the full-precision accuracy. With both at 4 bits, the models stay within 2.59 points of full precision, shrink their memory footprint 7.8--7.9 times, and use 6.4--6.9 times less energy.

Manoj Twarakavi, Venkata Sriram Siddhardh Nadendla
Advanced persistent threats (APTs) are a major concern in federated learning (FL) deployments in critical sectors such as healthcare, and finance. Traditional defense mechanisms fail to contain APTs due to their intermittent attacking behavior. This paper addresses a specific type of APT called covert model poisoning (CMP) where the attacker intermittently injects poisoned model updates in a covert manner. The interaction between the FL server and a CMP attacker is modeled as an imperfect repeated game where both players cannot observe each other's actions. A novel adversarial search algorithm called StratFL is designed alongside novel belief update algorithms at both the server and adversary. Experiments are designed using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets to evaluate and compare StratFL's performance against state-of-the-art methods. Empirical convergence of belief update algorithms is demonstrated across various security vignettes. At the same time, StratFL is found to exhibit an improved accuracy of 10% compared to state-of-the-art methods.

A recent result by Loff and Skomra showed that, for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on an ergodic graph, a variant of policy iteration runs in smoothed polynomial time. We do this by defining a condition number that naturally generalizes theirs, showing that sufficiently-perturbed games are well-conditioned with high probability, and showing that their algorithms are efficient on well-conditioned instances. Although the outline is similar, our proof requires a substantially new approach, based on log-Lipschitz distributions which recently appeared in work on the smoothed analysis of the simplex method. For our second contribution, we propose three new value iteration algorithms for solving deterministic mean-payoff games (also on any graph). All three are based on iterative methods for finding fixed points of non-expansive operators, which we show can be applied to the Shapley operator. A widely repeated intuition explains why: seeing the opponent's fresh strategy should act like optimism. We treat this intuition as a testable hypothesis about deterministic two-player zero-sum self-play dynamics and find that its canonical additive form fails an information-matched test. On an analytic witness family we compare alternating RM$^{+}$ against a one-sided predictive RM$^{+}$ that receives the same information channel each round and differs only in where the fresh signal enters, a persistent regret state versus a transient prediction term. Our main result is a dichotomy theorem that reduces trajectory separation to the recurrence of exact-vertex play by the predictive dynamics: under an interior-band assumption on the alternating iterate, either vertex times recur and the profile distance is at least, infinitely often, an explicit constant that our measurements nearly attain, or they terminate. Across the tested self-play regimes, any correct explanation of the alternation speedup must reproduce a staleness cost present at the smallest tested stale fraction, an advantage that persists across seven orders of payoff conditioning, regime crossings of the optimism family, and a measured per-perturbation cost of weakening the injection path that is far steeper for staleness than for partial persistence.

This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. ☆ Approximating the Value of Time-Bounded Weighted Timed Games

The Value Problem for weighted timed games, an extension of timed automata with weights and adversity, consists in determining, given a weighted timed game with a reachability objective and a rational threshold, whether or not the value of the game exceeds the threshold. This problem is known to be undecidable for weighted timed games, i.e., there is no algorithm that can compute the value exactly. A natural alternative is to approximate the value; however, the Approximation problem is also undecidable in general. In this paper, we prove that the Approximation problem is decidable in 4-ExpTime for weighted timed games whose executions are time-bounded.

In each period, the seller chooses a price from a set of predefined prices consisting of an original price and a few discounted price levels. The goal is to estimate the demand gradient at the original price to adjust the original price and improve revenue after the experiment. In our model, in each period, a unit mass of buyers arrives on the market, with values distributed based on a time-varying process. Crucially, buyers are forward-looking with a discounted utility and will choose not to purchase now if they expect to face a discounted price in the near future. We show that such forward-looking behavior introduces bias in naive estimators of the demand gradient, due to intertemporal interference. Furthermore, although experiments with only two price points are common in practice, we prove that no estimator using data from such experiments can recover the correct demand gradient, even in the limit of an infinitely long experiment with an infinitesimal price discount. Moreover, we characterize the form of the bias of naive estimators. Finally, we show that with a simple three-price-level experiment, the seller can remove the bias due to strategic forward-looking behavior and construct an estimator for the demand gradient that asymptotically recovers the truth. Our results provide practical guidance for platforms to obtain unbiased demand gradients from price experiments in the presence of forward-looking demand.

Our algorithm for the in-degree parameterization is particularly involved and technically intricate. Hence, our results offer a new perspective and significantly broaden the parameterized algorithmic understanding of the \textsc{Tournament Fixing} problem.

Such tournaments are used in sports and provide models for elections and organizational decision-making. Although the problem is NP-hard in general, it is polynomial-time solvable when some structural parameters become zero. Motivated by these cases, we study its parameterized complexity using those structural parameters centered on the favorite player. We prove fixed-parameter tractability when parameterized by either the number of players who beat the favorite player or the number that the favorite player beats. We next consider four subset parameters that measure the arc or vertex deletions needed to eliminate cycles through the player or either neighborhood. For each parameter, the problem remains NP-hard even when its value is one. When both neighborhoods are acyclic, we show that the problem remains NP-hard. We also give some sufficient conditions for the existence of a winning seeding. Our results complete the tractability classification of several individual parameters centered on the favorite player, extending the parameterized complexity landscape of this problem.

We propose a delay-signature framework in which the axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch or a small neuron's soma constitute a physical key: only input sequences whose spike-time differences the delays compensate arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection, a threshold on input summed within an inhibition-compressed window, converts that synchrony into an all-or-none output. First, in simulations of an integrator-neuron model, a single physical scalar -- the dispersion of the delay set -- moves a population from event to order-selective sequence detection. The transition is emergent under random delays and connectivity, and an exact calculation reproduces it: at narrow dispersion, sequence detectors do not exist, and the dispersion at which they overtake event detectors tracks the inter-event interval. This maps a computational distinction onto the anatomical one between myelinated and unmyelinated projections, making myelination a switch on what a neuron computes. Second, the same dispersion sets the code's limits: it bounds the longest codable interval and fixes an absolute timing tolerance of order a millisecond, the same at every dispersion. Third, that millisecond window and the conduction velocity of afferents inside cortex together set column diameter, and column anatomy predicts the window measured in mouse barrel cortex. One anatomically measurable parameter thus shapes what a neuron detects and sets the limits of what it can represent.
comment: 33 pages, 4 figures; submitted to PLOS Computational Biology
♻ ☆ Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine NeurIPS 2026
Thomas Hannagan
The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Thinking steps are attracting but strongly non-normal maps exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state thus has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

♻ ☆ Adaptive Domain Models: Bayesian Evolution, Warm Rotation, and Principled Training for Geometric and Neuromorphic AI
Houston Haynes
Transformer-based large language models have become a prominent focus of machine learning. We develop adaptive domain models to supply domain-specific predictions and checks within language-model pipelines, as well as to serve direct machine automation efficiently. Their predictions can inform generation, while declared constraints and error bounds support checks on the calculations underlying proposed responses and actions. These feedforward and feedback paths aim to reduce domain errors while supporting use cases such as constraint solving for machine processes as well as preserving accuracy in a language model's conversational setting. Physical dimensions and geometric support restrict admissible computation, while a probability model expresses uncertainty. Our type and program hypergraph work connects these relationships to numerical and deployment obligations. We derive a natural-gradient calculation over forward tangent directions using a declared program metric, with a calibration example and a bound separating metric, derivative and solve errors. Forward differentiation and posit accumulation expose complementary resource and error tradeoffs. Our worked linear-Gaussian update connects posterior computation to error and a distribution-shift decision. Recent results from Urschel bound elimination growth probabilistically under distinct Gaussian-input and random-preconditioning hypotheses. Our unique approach to warm rotation binds candidate parameters to their numerical evidence and destination while each request observes a coherent model and state. We propose Bayesian distillation as a source of prior information. Our architecture offers a route to domain computations with explicit guarantees that can guide automated decisions and model responses. We specify experiments to evaluate prediction quality, domain errors across conversational turns, and total resource cost.

Computer Science and Game Theory
☆ Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
Shubhendu Trivedi, Jacob Eisenstein, Alekh Agarwal, Ian Gemp, Michael Kaisers, Adam Fisch
An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

☆ What Does Disagreement Mean? A Semantic Identifiability Frontier for Pairwise Preference Learning ICML 2026
Manoj Saravanan, Rohit Kumar Salla, Shrikar Reddy Kota
Pairwise comparison data are a standard supervision signal in preference learning, but disagreement in such data can reflect stable latent heterogeneity, ephemeral stochasticity, or non-binary responses hidden by a forced-choice interface. We study which of these semantic distinctions are identifiable from the feedback channel itself. We introduce a nonparametric latent semantic model with three querywise quantities: aggregate directional preference $μ_q$, persistent disagreement $τ_q$, and non-binary mass $α_q$. Under the anonymous binary channel, we prove an exact semantic fiber theorem: $μ_q$ is point-identified, whereas $(τ_q, α_q)$ vary over an explicit feasible region compatible with the same binary law. Same-annotator repeats identify $τ_q$ through a covariance identity, abstention-enabled feedback identifies $α_q$ directly, and together they point-identify the full semantic triple. We also derive finite-sample estimators, nonasymptotic concentration bounds, and semantics-aware action-recovery guarantees, and validate the theory on theorem-matched synthetic data.

☆ Auction-based allocation of routes in capacity-constrained networks
Gergely Csáji, Dávid Csercsik
We study the route-set allocation problem between end nodes in capacity-constrained flow networks with transfer costs. We introduce an origin--destination (OD) bidding language, in which a participant bids for bounded conic combinations of inlet--outlet--quantity licences and the mechanism performs the routing through a network-flow optimising winner-determination problem. We then study payment rules for the OD mechanism. Under a restricted model with openly and uniformly priced sources and bidders who are indifferent to the source of the gas, the Vickrey--Clarke--Groves (VCG) payment is core-stable; the key structural fact is that in this regime some optimal aggregate flows never use a physical pipe in both directions, so the winner-determination problem reduces to a single-commodity network flow whose value is submodular in the set of active bidders. If source access is allowed to depend on the individual consumer -- a realistic feature, e.g. when gas deals are embedded in bilateral political bargaining -- the reduction fails and VCG payments may lie strictly outside the core. For this general model we propose a dual (nodal) pricing rule derived from the shadow prices of the flow-conservation constraints, and prove it is always core-stable, at the cost of dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. Illustrative examples accompany each result.
☆ No-Regret Learning in Stackelberg Security Games with an Unknown, Bounded Set of Attacker Types
Sabil Ahmad, Ishita, Aditi Singh, Swaprava Nath
In a repeated Stackelberg security game, a defender commits in every round to a randomized allocation of its resources, and an attacker, drawn from a set of types, best-responds. Existing no-regret guarantees assume that the defender knows this set of types in advance. We drop this assumption: the set of types is unknown, and its size is at most $K_{\max}$, an upper bound that the defender is not told. We show that what can be learned then depends on what the defender observes. If it observes the type of each attacker, an algorithm that adds types to its list as they appear achieves regret $\tilde O(nK_{\max}\sqrt{T})$ over $T$ rounds with $n$ targets, the same $\sqrt T$ rate as with known types, at an extra factor of only $\sqrt{K_{\max}}$ and without ever using $K_{\max}$. If it observes only the attacked target and types come from an infinite universe, no algorithm has sublinear regret: in a fixed three-target game every algorithm suffers regret at least $T-2$, even against a single attacker type, because it cannot tell which type it faces. If, in addition, it is told every $B$ rounds which types have appeared so far, sublinear regret returns, at $\tilde O(nK_{\max}^{4/3}T^{2/3}+K_{\max} B)$. The first term is the rate of the partial-information learner we use, and we show that the additive cost of the delay cannot be avoided.

☆ Accord: Schelling-Point Arbitration as a Composable Solana Primitive
Fabian Schuh
Accord is an arbitration oracle on Solana. Any Solana program can create an application specific court (i.e. subaccord) and file disputes. A random jury of a specialized, stake-weighted juror pool reviews encrypted evidence and votes under commit--reveal. Jurors that vote with the final ruling earn fees and slashed stake. Jurors that vote against it lose stake. Appeals grow the panel stepwise from 3 to 31 jurors, which raises both the cost of maintaining a captured verdict and, under certain conditions, the probability of a correct majority. Each pool defines its own collateral mint and its own fee mint, so the economics can fit the application. This paper elaborates the mechanism, the incentive model, the residual trust assumptions, and the differences to the established court on EVM, Kleros. We further discuss implementation details that are Solana specific.

☆ Optimal Online Stochastic Matching
Paul Duetting, Michal Feldman, Mathieu Molina
We resolve the problem of unweighted online stochastic matching with a known arrival law by establishing its optimal competitive ratio. For Poisson arrivals, we achieve $1-e/e^e\approx0.8206$, matching the upper bound of Chierichetti, Giacchini, Panconesi, and Vattani [ICALP 2025]. For exactly $n$ i.i.d.~arrivals, we obtain the same guarantee up to an additive $O(n^{-1/2})$ loss. Our key technical contribution is an exact correspondence between Poisson matching and exponential scheduling, preserving both online performance and the expected offline optimum. To prove the latter, we show that the distribution of the maximum of a random supermodular set function is determined by its joint distributions along chains of nested sets, a result of independent interest. This reduces the analysis to chains, where classical Poisson--exponential duality applies. The offline equivalence extends to arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. We then design a posterior allocation policy for exponential scheduling and use the correspondence to transfer its optimal competitive guarantee to online matching. Additionally, we show that the optimal competitive ratio under an unknown arrival law is strictly lower than $1-e/e^e$, establishing a strict separation between the known and unknown arrival models.
☆ Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
Yasushi Kawase, Bodhayan Roy, Mohammad Azharuddin Sanpui
We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.
comment: A preliminary version of this paper appeared in the proceedings of the 51st International Symposium on Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science (MFCS 2026)
☆ Effective-Balance Design in Ethereum Proof-of-Stake
Bolin Zhang, Xuechao Wang
Proof-of-Stake (PoS) systems offer a scalable and energy-efficient alternative to Proof-of-Work (PoW). The economic security of PoS relies critically on incentivizing broad and meaningful participation through well-cali\-brated staking reward mechanisms. We study Ethe\-reum's effective-balance rules as a mechanism-design problem in which the protocol chooses a reward coefficient, an activation threshold, and a maximum effective balance, and validators respond in the induced propor\-tional-allocation game. For fixed participating validators and identity counts, we establish a unique Nash equilibrium in validator-level total stakes. When validators can split or merge their visible identities, each candidate identity structure must be evaluated after the market re-clears. Restructuring incentives therefore depend on post-reset payoff comparisons that account for all validators' stake responses. For an illustrative simulation, we construct address-level budget proxies from Beacon Chain deposits and withdrawals, Lido staking flows, Etherscan balances, and calibrated synthetic agents. With illustrative cost coefficients, lowering the reserve price from 32 ETH to 30 ETH increases active identities by 5.922\% and total effective stake by 0.098\%.
☆ PPAD-Completeness of Contiguous Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Additive Valuations
Yasushi Kawase, Bodhayan Roy, Mohammad Azharuddin Sanpui
We prove that computing a complete contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free cake allocation is PPAD-complete for normalized rational piecewise-constant additive valuations. The hardness holds even when $\varepsilon$ is given in unary, and even when every density takes only two values, which are the same for all agents, and is piecewise constant with at most six breakpoints. As a consequence, computing an exact contiguous envy-free allocation is also PPAD-complete, and the hardness holds under the same restrictions on the densities. Our key ingredient is to assign prices to the pieces so that, in every approximately envy-free allocation, all prices are nearly equal, regardless of how the pieces are assigned to the agents. We further show that, for every fixed integer $c\ge1$, computing a contiguous EF$c$ allocation of indivisible goods on a path is PPAD-complete for additive valuations, and the hardness holds even for binary valuations in which each good is valued by exactly one agent and all agents value the same number of goods.
comment: We prove that computing a contiguous envy-free cake division is PPAD-complete for additive valuations, and that computing a contiguous EF$c$ allocation of goods on a path is PPAD-complete for every fixed $c \geq 1$, resolving open questions of Goldberg, Hollender and Suksompong (JAIR 2020) and Bilò et al.\ (ITCS 2019)
♻ ☆ Introspectively Envy-Free and Efficient Allocation of Indivisible Mixed Manna
Siddharth Barman, Paritosh Verma
The existence of allocations that are simultaneously fair and efficient is a central inquiry in fair division. Prominent results show that these complementary desiderata can be achieved together for indivisible items with nonnegative values. In particular, for indivisible goods and additive valuations, there always exists an allocation that is both envy-free up to one item (EF1) and fractionally Pareto efficient (fPO). An analogous EF1 and fPO guarantee is now known for indivisible chores. For indivisible mixed manna, the compatibility of fairness and efficiency is more delicate. Indeed, recent work shows that EF1 and fPO are incompatible in the additive mixed-manna setting. Through principled relaxations of EF1, we show that compatibility with fPO can be restored even for indivisible mixed manna under additive valuations. For indivisible mixed manna and additive valuations, we establish the existence of allocations that are fPO and introspectively envy-free up to one item (IEF1). In an IEF1 allocation, each agent can eliminate its envy toward every other agent by either adding an item to or removing an item from its own bundle. The notion of IEF1 coincides with EF1 for indivisible chores, and hence our result generalizes the existence guarantee for chores. We also prove the existence of allocations that are fPO and satisfy a chiral version of IEF1, which we call extrospectively envy-free up to one item (XEF1). This result generalizes the existence guarantee of EF1 and fPO allocations for goods, since XEF1 is equivalent to EF1 for goods. Finally, we utilize our IEF1 and fPO result for indivisible items to provide a distinct proof of the known EF and fPO guarantee for divisible mixed manna. Our results underscore the power of the Knaster--Kuratowski--Mazurkiewicz Theorem for proving the existence of fair and efficient allocations of indivisible and divisible items.
♻ ☆ Tourist arrival forecasting with game-theoretic social influence weighting and deep learning
Ali Nikseresht
In the era of Industry 5.0, data-driven decision-making has become indispensable for planning in service systems such as tourism. This paper proposes a non-linear hybrid approach for forecasting tourist arrivals to Hong Kong from five major source markets before COVID-19 and to Sanya, China, through the COVID-19 shock. The method integrates multiple sources of Internet big data and employs a cooperative game-theoretic algorithm to identify coalitions of opinion leaders on social media, whose content then receives larger weights. The Empirical Wavelet Transform (EWT), applied causally, manages nonstationary attributes, and a Stacked Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (Stacked BiLSTM) network tuned by Bayesian optimization generates the forecasts. We prove that the Shapley values of the underlying trust-weighted coverage game have a closed form and that the coalition of maximal synergy can be found exactly in polynomial time. Relative to the same network fed only with past arrivals, Internet big data reduce the one-step-ahead root mean squared error by 4.1-41.7% across the Hong Kong markets and opinion-leader weighting by a further 10.1-49.4%, against 5.3% and 8.7% for Sanya. The approach compares favorably with published benchmarks and remains robust under volatile conditions, which suggests uses in logistics, supply chains and production planning.
♻ ☆ Incentivize Contribution and Learn Parameters Too: Federated Learning with Strategic Data Owners
Drashthi Doshi, Avishek Ghosh, Swaprava Nath
In federated learning (FL), a center trains a shared model from updates that clients compute on their private data. Collecting and training on data is costly, so a strategic client may contribute little data and free-ride on the model trained by the others. We study mechanisms that incentivize data contribution and learn the model at the same time. Our first mechanism, UPBReD, updates the clients ' contributions and the model jointly, and converges at a geometric rate to a Nash equilibrium of the contribution game together with the welfare-maximizing model for those contributions. This equilibrium can involve under-contribution, so our second mechanism, 2P-UPBReD, adds budget-balanced transfers that make full contribution a dominant strategy, after which training converges to the optimal model; we also give conditions under which every client prefers to participate. Both mechanisms trust what clients report about the data they use and the gradients they compute. We show that no payment rule can reward unverifiable contributions unless something the center observes depends on the data actually used. Building on this, T-2P-UPBReD checks each client's reported contribution against the other clients ' realized valuations of the trained model, and prices gradient reports with a budget-balanced charge. It elicits truthful contribution reports, makes gradient reports approximately truthful, still reaches full contribution and the optimal model, and never runs a deficit. Experiments on CIFAR-10, FEMNIST, and Twitter show that 2P-UPBReD matches the welfare of FedAvg trained on all data, while strategic clients without incentives lower the welfare of the learned model.

♻ ☆ Likes, Budgets, and Equilibria: Designing Contests for Socially Optimal Advertising
Sayantika Mandal, Swaprava Nath
We study competitive advertising on a social network. Each of $m$ firms allocates a budget across consumers, and a platform decides, through a contest success function (CSF), what share of each consumer's attention every firm captures; awareness then spreads through the network. We model awareness and budgets on two timescales and bound how many fast steps awareness needs to settle between budget updates. On the slow timescale, best-response dynamics converge at a geometric rate to a Nash equilibrium whenever the firms' utilities are strongly concave and smooth, and a subclass of the standard ratio-form CSFs satisfies these conditions. Their equilibrium, however, need not maximize welfare: a firm's spending lowers its rivals' shares of attention, so individual and social optima differ, and a constant per-unit charge cannot close this gap in general. We give a sufficient condition for the equilibrium to coincide with the welfare optimum. To meet it, we multiply each firm's ratio share by a function of the total spending at the consumer, a class we call scaled ratio CSFs (SRCSFs), and show that within this class the condition holds exactly when this function is a power of the total spending, which gives the Power RCSF. The Power RCSF alone falls short in two ways. Its equilibrium is optimal only when firms exhaust their budgets, which we remove with a budget-balanced per-unit charge. Its curvature also becomes unbounded as spending at a consumer approaches zero, breaking convergence, which we restore by requiring every firm to spend a small minimum on each consumer. With both additions, best-response dynamics converge to a unique, symmetric equilibrium that maximizes $p$-mean social welfare for every $p \le 1$ simultaneously, so the Price of Anarchy is one.

☆ Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
Alban Gattepaille, Alexandre Muzy
Exploiting temporal information in datasets with high temporal dependencies (such as spoken keyword recognition) by spiking models is still an open problem. Promising frameworks include Time-To-First coding (TTFS) and the inclusion of synaptic delays into learning. In TTFS, neurons are forced to spike at most once, forcing the network to found its learning on the spiking times of neurons rather than their spiking rate. Some models use the TTFS framework to directly compute the spiking time of Integrate-and-Fire (IF) or Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons. However, most models built in the TTFS framework have not been tested against datasets containing temporal information. Little is known about the latency of these models on temporal datasets, where the latency is the time taken by the network to correctly classify a sample. In this work, we study the behaviour of Delay Neural Networks (DeNN) models, i.e. models that directly compute the spiking time of neurons by bypassing the membrane potential and thresholding mechanisms of spiking neurons. We show how to analytically control their latency, and empirically study the latency-accuracy tradeoff in a dynamic temporal dataset.

This study tests whether the name predicts the result. Eighteen configurations were run at 5,000 evaluations under three population allocations, with statistics fixed in advance. Four NSGA-II implementations differed by up to 5% in hypervolume, more than three canonical algorithms of different families differed from one another, and their response to population size differed by up to 10 percentage points; for two MOEA/D implementations, by 28. On ZDT test functions the same NSGA-II implementations differed up to 470-fold in IGD. An ablation in one open-source NSGA-II reproduced the behaviour of one tool from its documented settings but not the gaps of the other two, so documented parameters do not identify an implementation. Counting the budget in wall-clock time reversed the ranking of the model-based optimizer, and reporting the final population instead of the archive understated some configurations by up to a third; most differences fell below the surrogate's error. For optimizers embedded in design-support systems, the implementation is part of the method; a reporting checklist is derived: implementation and version, effective settings, budget in time and evaluations, and archive-based indicators.

☆ Design and Analysis of Temporal Representations in Neural Networks
Alban Colas-Gattepaille, Alexandre Muzy
The ability to represent temporal information is often hypothesized to underlie the efficiency and learning capabilities of biological neural networks. This motivates the development of spiking neural networks. However, it remains unclear how temporal information is actually represented in neural networks and how different forms of temporal representation affect performance and computational efficiency. We introduce the notion of the degree of temporal representation of a neural network, defined by whether its constituent functions (activation, learning, encoding, and decoding) explicitly manipulate time as a computational variable. This perspective yields a continuum ranging from non-temporal representations, where time does not explicitly appear as a computational variable in the network functions, to fully temporal representations, where computations explicitly operate on temporal variables. Using a fixed deep architecture, we compare different encoding, activation mechanisms and decoding with increasing temporal expressiveness: non-temporal weighted-sum activations used in usual artificial neural networks, non-temporal binary spiking activations used in spiking neural networks, and spike-time-based activations used in delay neural networks. Experiments on event-based datasets show that increasing the degree of temporal representation improves both performance and computational efficiency, allowing state-of-the-art performances on the Google Speech Commands dataset. We further analyze how temporal representations induce distinct forward and backward computational trajectories, leading to gradients that depend explicitly on the history of event times.
☆ A Time-Variant Spiking Neuron from a Unified State-Dynamics Perspective
Jing Yang, Qianhui Liu, Gang Pan, Zhanglu Yan
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have increasingly incorporated rich neuronal dynamics to enhance temporal processing. However, richer dynamics do not necessarily enable neurons to adapt how information is processed over time. To examine this issue systematically, we introduce a unified state-dynamics framework that characterizes diverse spiking neurons through a common formulation and enables direct comparison of their dynamical designs. The framework reveals a common limitation of existing neurons: although they enhance temporal processing through richer internal states and state evolution, the dynamical rules determining how inputs are integrated, how states evolve, and how they are read out generally remain unchanged throughout temporal processing. Such time-invariant rules limit the ability of neurons to adjust information processing as information relevance changes over time. Inspired by time-varying regulation in biological neurons, we propose the Time-Variant Multi-Compartment Neuron (TV-MCN). TV-MCN builds on multiscale compartment dynamics and makes the rules for input integration, state evolution, and state readout time-varying according to the current input. Specifically, an input-dependent internal time regulates the rate of state evolution, while the current input dynamically modulates input integration and state readout. Extensive experiments show that TV-MCN achieves strong overall performance, with particularly large gains on tasks requiring selective retention and retrieval of information, while ablation studies further support the effectiveness of its time-varying mechanisms.
☆ How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
